mixture-of-experts.name: Mixture of experts
mixture-of-experts.definition: A layer containing several parameterized expert functions and a router that selects which experts process each input.
mixture-of-experts.explanation: An MoE layer increases parameter capacity while activating only a subset of experts per token. Each expert can be an ordinary feed-forward network; this chapter uses scalar linear experts so every gradient is visible. The router produces probabilities and a sparse dispatch decision. Conditional computation can reduce arithmetic relative to evaluating every expert, but routing, communication, imbalance, and memory still cost resources. A tiny CPU layer does not demonstrate large-scale efficiency.

router.name: Router
router.definition: A learned function that scores experts for each input and determines sparse dispatch.
router.explanation: The chapter's router is a matrix mapping a two-feature input to three logits, followed by stable softmax and top-1 selection. The argmax index is piecewise constant, so gradients do not pass through a change of selected index. They do pass through the selected full-softmax probability used in the output. A separate balancing term supplies another gradient based on average probabilities and observed assignment frequencies.

conditional-compute.name: Conditional computation
conditional-compute.definition: Evaluating only selected model components for a particular input.
conditional-compute.explanation: Dense layers run every parameter for every token. Sparse MoE routing chooses one or a few experts, so different tokens activate different parameters. The potential saving depends on expert size and system overhead. The reference executes only one selected expert per accepted example, but still computes all three small router scores. It measures correctness and learning; it does not claim a speedup because the fixture is far too small and has no distributed communication.

expert-capacity.name: Expert capacity
expert-capacity.definition: The maximum number of tokens an expert accepts from one routing group or batch.
expert-capacity.explanation: Capacity is based on tokens divided by experts times a capacity factor; this project explicitly rounds up and bounds it below by one. It turns uneven routing into an explicit resource limit. Once an expert is full, later assigned tokens overflow. The reference counts them and omits their expert task update; large residual architectures may pass dropped tokens through a residual path. Higher capacity reduces dropping while allocating more temporary space and computation.

load-balancing-loss.name: Load-balancing loss
load-balancing-loss.definition: An auxiliary MoE objective that sums, across experts, attempted hard-assignment frequency times mean router probability, multiplied by the expert count and coefficient; hard frequencies are stop-gradient while probabilities remain differentiable.
load-balancing-loss.explanation: The attempted hard-assignment frequencies count every route before capacity admission and divide by all T examples. Mean probabilities also use the full softmax over all T examples. Capacity acceptance and dropped-token metrics stay separate from this objective. The term discourages collapse but does not guarantee semantically useful specialization, and its coefficient must be reported rather than hidden in training code.

top-k-routing.name: Top-k routing
top-k-routing.definition: Selecting the k highest-scoring experts for each input.
top-k-routing.explanation: Top-1 minimizes expert evaluations. If its sole selected probability is divided by itself, the gate becomes exactly one and task loss has zero local derivative with respect to router logits. Keeping the selected full-softmax probability avoids that failure. Top-2 can instead renormalize two selected weights: their relative softmax still changes with both logits when expert outputs differ. The discrete membership boundary remains nondifferentiable in either design.
